internship.title: Frontend Web Development Internship
internship.description: A research-grounded internship focused specifically on frontend web development: browser fundamentals, semantic HTML, CSS, JavaScript, TypeScript, React, responsive UI, accessibility, application architecture, testing, security, performance, Git and production-oriented delivery.

duration.basis: Estimated at roughly 15–20 focused hours/week; actual time varies with prior experience. This is a workload estimate, not a guaranteed duration.

prerequisites: Basic computer literacy and terminal/editor use.
objectives: Understand the web platform rather than treating frameworks as magic.
Debug, test, secure, measure and document frontend work.
Complete a substantial internship-specific final project.

modules.title: Web Platform, Tooling and Professional Workflow
modules.description: Browser mental model, DevTools, npm/Vite and professional Git habits.
objectives: Explain the roles of HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
Use DevTools to reproduce and diagnose UI defects.
Create reproducible projects with npm and Vite.
Use focused Git changes and review practices.

lessons.title: How the Web Page Becomes a Running Interface
lessons.description: Build a practical browser mental model.
learningObjectives: Describe document, style and behavior layers.
Identify where frontend defects can originate.
lessons.notes: HTML supplies structure and semantics; CSS supplies presentation; JavaScript adds behavior. Tooling transforms and serves these platform primitives. Debugging starts by identifying which layer owns the symptom.

lessons.title: DevTools as an Engineering Instrument
lessons.description: Use browser tools for evidence-driven debugging.
learningObjectives: Use breakpoints, Console and Network tools.
lessons.notes: A reproducible symptom plus browser evidence is stronger than trial-and-error. Elements answers what rendered, Computed explains winning styles, Sources/Console expose runtime behavior, and Network exposes resource failures.
practicals: Reproduce a CSS overflow bug and fix it using evidence from the box model and Computed styles.

lessons.title: npm, Vite and Reproducible Setup
lessons.description: Understand package scripts, dependencies and builds.
lessons.notes: Vite supplies a development server and production build pipeline. A manifest records direct dependencies and scripts; a lockfile makes dependency resolution reproducible. Use an LTS Node.js release for production-oriented work.

quiz.question: What is Vite in this internship?
options: Frontend build tool and dev server
quiz.answer: Frontend build tool and dev server
quiz.explanation: Vite provides development and production build tooling.

lessons.title: Git Workflow for Frontend Work
lessons.description: Make changes reviewable and attributable.
lessons.notes: Never commit credentials, environment secrets or dependency directories. A good review checks behavior, accessibility, maintainability, tests and regression risk.
practicals: Create a branch, make one UI change, inspect the diff and write a short review checklist.

tasks.title: Debug a Layout Regression
tasks.description: Diagnose a narrow-viewport overflow using DevTools.
tasks.problemStatement: A content panel overflows its parent on narrow viewports. Identify the rule, explain the evidence and make the smallest fix.
tasks.solutionCode: Use flexible sizing rather than masking overflow.

tasks.title: Prepare a Reviewable Change
tasks.description: Turn a small UI improvement into a focused Git change.
tasks.problemStatement: Add an empty state and prepare a branch, commit and review notes.
tasks.hint:
git switch -c feat/empty-state
git diff --check
git add src/
git commit -m "feat: add empty state to task list"
git show --stat --oneline HEAD
tasks.solutionCode: The workflow makes the change reviewable and avoids unrelated files.

modules.title: Semantic HTML, Forms and Accessibility Foundations
modules.description: Build accessible structure, forms, keyboard interaction and WCAG-aware review habits.
objectives: Use WCAG 2.2 as a practical reference.

lessons.title: Semantic HTML and Document Structure
lessons.description: Use headings, landmarks, links, buttons and lists correctly.
lessons.notes: Semantic controls provide browser and assistive-technology behavior without custom JavaScript. Use buttons for actions and links for navigation.

quiz.question: Which element is preferred for an action that changes application state?
quiz.explanation: A button is a semantic action control.

lessons.title: Accessible Forms and Validation
lessons.description: Create labeled, understandable forms.
lessons.notes: A form should remain understandable without CSS. Labels, native input types and useful error text create a strong baseline. Do not rely on color alone for errors.
practicals: Build a contact form with labels, native constraints and an accessible error summary.

lessons.title: Keyboard Access, Focus and ARIA
lessons.description: Design interactions that work without a mouse.
lessons.notes: Keyboard accessibility is interaction design. ARIA should add semantics only when native HTML cannot express the required pattern; adding a role does not automatically implement keyboard behavior.

quiz.question: What should be preferred before adding a custom ARIA role?
options: Native HTML element with needed semantics
quiz.answer: Native HTML element with needed semantics
quiz.explanation: Native elements include built-in semantics and interaction behavior.

lessons.title: WCAG 2.2 and Human Accessibility Testing
lessons.description: Combine automated checks with human evaluation.
learningObjectives: Explain the role of WCAG success criteria.
lessons.notes: WCAG 2.2 contains testable success criteria but does not guarantee every user need. Automated tools detect some classes of problems; human testing is still required for focus order, wording and interaction.

tasks.title: Repair an Inaccessible Form
tasks.description: Refactor placeholder-only labels and generic click controls.
tasks.problemStatement: Make the form keyboard and assistive-technology friendly.
requirements: Do not rely on color alone.
tasks.hint:
<form>
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required autocomplete="email" />
  <button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>
tasks.solutionCode: Native form semantics provide accessible names and keyboard behavior.

tasks.title: Accessibility Code Review
tasks.description: Review a component for semantics, keyboard and feedback defects.
tasks.problemStatement: Find at least five defects and propose corrected behavior.
constraints: Tab through it before reading code.
tasks.solutionCode: Use native controls and explicit state semantics.

modules.title: CSS Architecture, Layout and Responsive Interfaces
modules.description: Use modern CSS to build maintainable, responsive layouts.
objectives: Design focus, state and reduced-motion styles.

lessons.title: Cascade, Specificity and Maintainable CSS
lessons.description: Diagnose why a CSS declaration wins.
lessons.notes: Use DevTools rather than adding selectors blindly. Keep selectors predictable and component-oriented.

lessons.title: Flexbox and Grid
lessons.description: Choose layout systems based on relationships.
lessons.notes: Flexbox is strong for one axis; Grid is strong for coordinated rows and columns. Intrinsic sizing, min-width and gap often matter more than fixed coordinates.
practicals: Build a dashboard header with Flexbox and a responsive card matrix with Grid.

lessons.title: Responsive Design and Mobile-First CSS
lessons.description: Create layouts that adapt to available space.
learningObjectives: Use fluid sizing and media queries.
lessons.notes: Responsive design is an approach, not a list of devices. Start with the narrow layout and introduce structural changes when content needs them.
practicals: Resize the capstone at narrow, tablet and desktop widths and record layout changes.

quiz.question: What should primarily determine a breakpoint?
options: Where the content needs to change
quiz.answer: Where the content needs to change

lessons.title: Motion, States and Reduced Motion
lessons.description: Create usable interaction states.
lessons.notes: Focus must remain visible. Motion should clarify state changes rather than decorate every interaction. Respect the user preference for reduced motion.
quiz: Add focus-visible styles and a reduced-motion media query.

tasks.title: Responsive Dashboard Shell
tasks.problemStatement: It must work from mobile through desktop without unwanted horizontal scrolling.
tasks.solutionCode: The layout uses CSS rather than viewport-dependent JavaScript.

tasks.title: CSS Refactor and Regression Review
tasks.description: Remove positional layout hacks while preserving states.
tasks.problemStatement: Replace normal-layout absolute positioning with Grid/Flexbox.
tasks.hint:
.toolbar { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: .75rem; }
.toolbar__actions { margin-inline-start: auto; display: flex; gap: .5rem; }
tasks.solutionCode: The refactor models relationships rather than coordinates.

modules.title: JavaScript for Interactive Web Applications
modules.description: Build reliable browser behavior with modules, async work, storage and defensive error handling.
objectives: Use modern JavaScript collections and functions.

lessons.title: Modern JavaScript Fundamentals
lessons.description: Model UI behavior with values, functions and collections.
lessons.notes: Treat frontend JavaScript as application code. Prefer clear transformations and immutable updates for state-like data.

quiz.question: Which operation transforms every item into a new array?

lessons.title: Modules and Separation of Concerns
lessons.description: Use ES modules to separate responsibilities.
learningObjectives: Separate domain, UI and storage code.
lessons.notes: A module should have a coherent reason to change. Keeping storage independent from React components makes testing and reasoning easier.

lessons.title: Async JavaScript and Fetch
lessons.description: Model loading, success and failure explicitly.
lessons.notes: fetch resolves when headers arrive even for HTTP error statuses, so response.ok/status must be checked before treating a response as successful.
practicals: Write a typed fetch helper that checks response.ok and converts unknown errors into user-safe messages.

lessons.title: Storage, Serialization and Defensive Errors
lessons.description: Persist optional client state safely.
lessons.notes: localStorage is not a secure database or secret store. JSON parsing can fail and stored shapes can be invalid, so validate before use and fall back safely.

tasks.title: Build a Typed Storage Adapter
tasks.description: Load, validate and save task data.
tasks.problemStatement: Stored JSON may be malformed or contain invalid status values.
constraints: Use unknown and a type guard.
tasks.solutionCode: Storage is treated as unreliable client input.

tasks.title: Network Failure State Machine
tasks.description: Model idle/loading/success/error states for async work.
tasks.problemStatement: Do not render failed responses as valid data.
tasks.hint:
type RequestState<T> = { status: 'idle' } | { status: 'loading' } | { status: 'success'; data: T } | { status: 'error'; message: string };
async function requestJson<T>(input: RequestInfo | URL): Promise<T> { const response = await fetch(input); if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Request failed with ${response.status}`); return await response.json() as T; }
tasks.solutionCode: The union makes impossible UI states harder to represent.

modules.title: TypeScript and React Fundamentals
modules.description: Build typed component-based interfaces with predictable state.
objectives: Model UI domain states with TypeScript.
Distinguish derived values from stored state.

lessons.title: TypeScript for UI Domain Models
lessons.description: Use unions and narrowing for UI data.
lessons.notes: Types describe intended shapes but do not validate runtime data. String unions are useful for finite status values.

quiz.question: Which type is safest before validating external data?
quiz.explanation: unknown forces validation before property access.

lessons.title: React Components, Props and Composition
lessons.description: Design focused components with explicit contracts.
lessons.notes: Choose component boundaries around cohesive behavior rather than arbitrary line counts.

lessons.title: State, Events and Hooks
lessons.description: Manage interactive state predictably.
learningObjectives: Use functional state updates when needed.
lessons.notes: Store the minimum information the UI needs to remember. Derive filtered lists and counts from source state rather than duplicating them.
quiz: Build a filter whose visible list is derived from query/status state.

lessons.title: Effects and Synchronization
lessons.description: Use effects for external synchronization.
lessons.notes: If a value can be computed during render, an effect usually adds unnecessary synchronization. Effects are for systems outside React.

quiz.question: What is the strongest reason to use an effect?
quiz.explanation: Effects coordinate React with external systems.

tasks.title: Refactor Untyped UI Data
tasks.description: Convert arbitrary status strings into a safe domain model.
constraints: Use a switch or explicit mapping.
tasks.hint:
export type TaskStatus = 'todo' | 'in-progress' | 'done';
export interface Task { id: string; title: string; status: TaskStatus; }
tasks.solutionCode: The type model makes invalid states visible.

tasks.title: Component Boundary Review
tasks.description: Split a monolithic component into focused components.
tasks.problemStatement: Separate orchestration, filters, list and dialog responsibilities.
constraints: Ask who reads and writes each value.
tasks.hint: type FilterBarProps = { query: string; status: TaskStatus | 'all'; onQueryChange: (value: string) => void; onStatusChange: (value: TaskStatus | 'all') => void; };
tasks.solutionCode: Explicit contracts make component boundaries maintainable.

modules.title: Frontend Application Architecture and Data Flow
modules.description: Combine components, state, persistence, forms and user feedback into a coherent application.

lessons.title: State Ownership and Data Flow
lessons.description: Trace state through user actions.
learningObjectives: Separate domain and derived UI state.
lessons.notes: State flows down and events flow up. Duplicate state creates synchronization bugs.

lessons.title: Forms, Dialogs and Focus Management
lessons.description: Build a testable accessible dialog.
lessons.notes: A dialog needs an accessible name and predictable focus behavior. For complex production dialogs, focus trapping and background inertness may be required; the capstone intentionally keeps the pattern small and testable.
practicals: Implement a create/edit dialog and verify keyboard-only interaction.

lessons.title: Client Persistence Without Pretending It Is a Backend
lessons.description: Use localStorage with explicit limitations.
lessons.notes: The capstone is frontend-only. localStorage demonstrates persistence but does not provide multi-user synchronization, authorization or server durability.

lessons.title: Error, Empty and Loading States
lessons.description: Design non-happy-path states.
lessons.notes: A serious interface explains zero records, invalid filters and storage failures. Error messages should be useful without exposing implementation details.

tasks.title: Task Dialog Feature
tasks.problemStatement: Validate before committing, support cancel, and preserve focus.
requirements: Do not mutate list before validation.
constraints: Keep draft state local to dialog.
tasks.hint: type TaskDialogProps = { open: boolean; mode: 'create' | 'edit'; onCancel: () => void; onSubmit: (draft: TaskDraft) => void; };
tasks.solutionCode: Draft state remains separate from committed task state.

tasks.title: Application Data-Flow Review
tasks.description: Trace task creation from click to persistence and render.
tasks.problemStatement: Document source of truth, validation boundary and storage boundary.
tasks.hint: User -> dialog draft -> validation -> parent task state -> storage adapter -> localStorage -> derived render
tasks.solutionCode: The diagram exposes the actual frontend-only architecture.

modules.title: Testing, Security, Performance and Production Readiness
modules.description: Verify frontend work responsibly before delivery.

lessons.title: Testing Strategy and Testable Design
lessons.description: Choose tests based on behavior and risk.
lessons.notes: Pure utilities are easy to unit test; components should be tested through user-visible behavior; E2E tests validate critical flows in a browser.

quiz.question: What should UI tests primarily verify?

lessons.title: Vitest and React Testing Library
lessons.description: Test domain logic and React interactions.
learningObjectives: Render components in a DOM environment.
lessons.notes: Vitest integrates with Vite; React Testing Library encourages tests that resemble user interaction.
practicals: Test filtering as a pure function and create-task behavior through labels.

lessons.title: Playwright End-to-End Testing
lessons.description: Validate critical workflows in browsers.
lessons.notes: Playwright Test provides browser isolation and cross-browser execution. Prefer locators and assertions over arbitrary sleeps.
practicals: Write an E2E test for create and filter behavior.

lessons.title: Frontend Security and Safe Rendering
lessons.description: Avoid common DOM XSS patterns.
lessons.notes: Normal React JSX rendering escapes string values, but escape hatches such as dangerouslySetInnerHTML can reintroduce risk. OWASP recommends safe DOM APIs and context-aware output handling.

quiz.question: Which is safest for an untrusted plain-text string?
quiz.explanation: Treat untrusted input as text, not markup or code.

lessons.title: Performance Measurement and Core Web Vitals
lessons.description: Measure LCP, INP and CLS.
learningObjectives: Explain the three Core Web Vitals.
Identify likely causes of slow interactions/layout shifts.
lessons.notes: Current Core Web Vitals focus on loading, interactivity and visual stability. Use measurement rather than invented benchmark claims.
practicals: Run a production build and use browser tooling to identify one measurable optimization opportunity.

lessons.title: Production Build, Deployment and Operational Checks
lessons.description: Prepare and verify a static production build.
lessons.notes: Vite outputs static assets. Provider-specific routing and deployment behavior must be checked against current provider documentation; this capstone has one root route.
practicals: Build the project, serve dist with a static server and perform smoke checks.

tasks.title: Test the Critical User Journey
tasks.problemStatement: Cover the riskiest user flows without implementation-detail assertions.
tasks.hint: test('filters tasks by status', () => { expect(filterTasks(tasks, { query: '', status: 'done' })).toHaveLength(1); });
tasks.solutionCode: Behavior-focused tests are resilient to refactoring.

tasks.title: Security and Performance Review
tasks.description: Review safe rendering, persistence limits and measurable performance risks.
tasks.problemStatement: Produce findings and remediation without fabricated benchmarks.
tasks.solutionCode: Safe text rendering avoids interpreting untrusted content as markup.

modules.title: Final Capstone — Accessible Responsive Issue Tracker Dashboard
modules.description: Complete the internship-specific capstone, validate it and explain the engineering decisions.
objectives: Integrate the full frontend skill set.
Demonstrate accessibility, testing, security and performance reasoning.

lessons.title: Capstone Delivery and Final Engineering Review
lessons.description: Run the release checklist and prepare the final handoff.
learningObjectives: Perform manual accessibility and responsive checks.
lessons.notes: A final project is complete only when the intern can explain state ownership, component boundaries, persistence, validation, tests, accessibility and security limitations. Unresolved issues should be documented honestly.

project.heading: Build an Accessible Responsive Issue Tracker Dashboard
project.description: Build a production-style single-page frontend for a small engineering team to capture, search, filter, edit and review work items. The project is intentionally frontend-only and uses localStorage for browser-local persistence so the intern demonstrates state architecture, accessibility, responsive design, testing, security-aware rendering and performance practices without inventing a backend.
project.problemStatement: A small team needs a dependable interface for managing work items across todo, in-progress and done states. The interface must remain usable on mobile, tablet and desktop, support keyboard users, communicate validation and empty states clearly, preserve work between browser sessions, and be structured so the code can be tested and maintained.
objectives: Translate requirements into maintainable React + TypeScript architecture.
Build semantic, keyboard-accessible and responsive UI.
Model and validate persisted task data.
Apply safe rendering and measure performance honestly.

functional: Display title, description, status and priority.
Create and edit tasks through an accessible dialog.
Search and filter without mutating source data.
Provide empty, validation and storage-error states.
technical: No backend or fabricated external API.
accessibility: Status not communicated by color alone.
Responsive layout without unwanted horizontal scrolling.
security: Do not confuse client validation with server trust.
performance: Measure production behavior before optimization claims.

features.name: Task overview
features.behavior: Derived counts for total, todo, in-progress and done.

features.name: Search and filtering
features.behavior: Filters the visible list by text and status.

features.name: Create task
features.behavior: Validates a draft and commits it only when valid.

features.name: Edit task
features.behavior: Edits a draft and commits one validated update.

features.name: Local persistence
features.behavior: Serializes valid records and safely recovers from malformed storage.

features.name: Responsive navigation
features.behavior: Uses CSS layout rather than viewport JavaScript.

features.name: Accessible feedback
features.behavior: Uses semantic headings, labels, focus and dialog semantics.

technologyStack.name: Vitest
technologyStack.why: Current package version was verified during research.

architecture.style: Component-based frontend with a single task state owner, pure domain utilities and a persistence adapter.
architecture.dataFlow: User -> React event -> validation -> state update -> storage adapter -> localStorage -> derived render
architecture.securityBoundary: Persisted records are untrusted client data; React renders strings as text and no HTML injection path exists.
architecture.responsiveStrategy: Mobile-first CSS with content-driven breakpoints and Grid/Flexbox.

# Accessible Responsive Issue Tracker

Frontend-only React + TypeScript internship capstone.

## Commands

`npm install`
`npx playwright install`
`npm run dev`
`npm run test`
`npm run build`
`npm run preview`
`npm run test:e2e`

## Scope and limitations

The application stores task records in browser localStorage. It is not a backend, authentication system, secure secret store, multi-user database or server durability mechanism. User-entered strings are rendered as text; no HTML injection APIs are used.

## Final verification

Perform keyboard, focus, responsive and console-error smoke checks. Run automated tests and the production build in an environment with dependencies installed. Do not claim performance or test results without running the measurement/test commands.

finalProject.heading: Build an Accessible Responsive Issue Tracker Dashboard
finalProject.description: Build a production-style single-page frontend for a small engineering team to capture, search, filter, edit and review work items. The project is intentionally frontend-only and uses localStorage for browser-local persistence so the intern demonstrates state architecture, accessibility, responsive design, testing, security-aware rendering and performance practices without inventing a backend.
finalProject.problemStatement: A small team needs a dependable interface for managing work items across todo, in-progress and done states. The interface must remain usable on mobile, tablet and desktop, support keyboard users, communicate validation and empty states clearly, preserve work between browser sessions, and be structured so the code can be tested and maintained.
objectives: Translate requirements into maintainable React + TypeScript architecture.
Build semantic, keyboard-accessible and responsive UI.
Model and validate persisted task data.
Apply safe rendering and measure performance honestly.

functional: Display title, description, status and priority.
Create and edit tasks through an accessible dialog.
Search and filter without mutating source data.
Provide empty, validation and storage-error states.
technical: No backend or fabricated external API.
accessibility: Status not communicated by color alone.
Responsive layout without unwanted horizontal scrolling.
security: Do not confuse client validation with server trust.
performance: Measure production behavior before optimization claims.

features.name: Task overview
features.behavior: Derived counts for total, todo, in-progress and done.

features.name: Search and filtering
features.behavior: Filters the visible list by text and status.

features.name: Create task
features.behavior: Validates a draft and commits it only when valid.

features.name: Edit task
features.behavior: Edits a draft and commits one validated update.

features.name: Local persistence
features.behavior: Serializes valid records and safely recovers from malformed storage.

features.name: Responsive navigation
features.behavior: Uses CSS layout rather than viewport JavaScript.

features.name: Accessible feedback
features.behavior: Uses semantic headings, labels, focus and dialog semantics.

architecture.style: Component-based frontend with a single task state owner, pure domain utilities and a persistence adapter.
architecture.dataFlow: User -> React event -> validation -> state update -> storage adapter -> localStorage -> derived render
architecture.securityBoundary: Persisted records are untrusted client data; React renders strings as text and no HTML injection path exists.
architecture.responsiveStrategy: Mobile-first CSS with content-driven breakpoints and Grid/Flexbox.

evaluation.approach: Evaluate demonstrated capability rather than arbitrary content volume.
evaluation.finalEvaluation: The intern passes when they can explain the architecture, demonstrate main flows, diagnose a defect, explain accessibility/security choices, run the verification workflow and honestly describe limitations. Completion does not guarantee employment or accreditation.

researchNotes.scopeBasis: The exact internship name is Frontend Web Development Internship; research was scoped to frontend/web technologies and engineering practices rather than backend or full-stack curriculum.
currentPracticeNotes: React 19.2 is the latest documented React line researched.
Vite 8.2.2 was verified as current npm release during research.
TypeScript 7.0.2 was verified as current stable npm release during research.
Node.js 24 was verified as LTS in the official release table while Node.js 26 was Current.
WCAG 2.2 was used as the accessibility standard reference.
Vitest and Playwright were selected from official testing documentation.
OWASP XSS guidance informed safe rendering and avoidance of dangerous DOM sinks.
Core Web Vitals informed performance topics; no benchmark result is claimed.
Vitest 5.0.0 was verified as the current npm package during final verification.
